result.markdown: --- title: "Ordinary differential equations" course-unit: ch03-ordinary-differential-equations status: complete --- ## Why this unit matters - Foundations solved SIR and established theory, here we will explore the Julia tools for solving ODEs. - We cover: building an `ODEProblem`, the `Tsit5` solver, dense interpolation `sol(t)`, **callbacks** for events, and `remake` for scenarios. - Two events: a time-limited **lockdown** and automatic **peak detection**. ## A lockdown is a piecewise-constant $\beta$ {.smaller} A lockdown does not add compartments or flows. What we expect from it is a drop in transmission that lasts as long as the restrictions do: $\beta$ falls at $t_1$ and returns at $t_2$. That makes $\beta$ a step function of time: $$ \beta(t)=\begin{cases}\beta_\text{lock}, & t_1\le t dIdt(u, integrator.p), # condition: zero at the peak integrator -> push!(peak_t, integrator.t)) # affect!: record the time ``` The solver then continuously monitors this number as it integrates through time and trigger the callback the exact instant the number crosses zero (changes sign from positive to negative, or vice versa) - **The state to test arrives as `u`.** That is why the condition takes `(u, t, integrator)` while the `affect!`, which runs once, takes the integrator alone. - **So `integrator.u` in a condition is a bug.** It is the state at the *end* of the step, identical at every trial, so the sign never changes and the event is never found. Julia will not warn you. - **Only a sign change counts.** A peak at $t_1$, $t_2$ or at an end of the span never passes through zero, so nothing fires. ::: {.notes} Contrast with the previous slide: nobody can write down the peak time in advance, but everyone can write down the condition that holds there. That is the case for a ContinuousCallback. The integrator.u trap is worth dwelling on because Julia does not complain. The code runs, the callback simply never fires, and people conclude their model has no peak. If a ContinuousCallback appears to do nothing, this is the first thing to check. There is a third argument for direction: ContinuousCallback(cond, up!, down!), and passing nothing for one of them fires on one direction only. Part C of the worksheet uses that to trigger restrictions on the way up but not on the way down. ::: ## Finding the peak: two ways {.smaller} $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t = 0$ can be found after the solve, or during it. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### After the simulation - Grid-bound: with `saveat = 0.5`, a peak at day 18.23 reads as 18.0 or 18.5. - `sol(t)` fixes the sharpness. Scan a fine grid of the interpolant, saving nothing extra. - Records only. It cannot change the run. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### During the simulation - Root-finds on the same dense interpolant, inside the step, to solver tolerance. - No grid to choose. - Can act, not only record. Ours only saves the number, but the same callback can drop $\beta$ the moment $I$ crosses capacity. ::: :::: ::: {.notes} This slide exists because someone will ask why we are not just using argmax, as session 1 did. The answer is not that argmax is wrong. It is used again on the validation slide as the reference the callback is checked against, so do not dismiss it here. The honest ranking of the reasons: sharpness is real but curable with sol(t); the sweep pattern with save_everystep = false is a genuine saving; and the one that cannot be worked around is the last bullet. A quantity computed after the fact cannot change the trajectory it was computed from. Be straight that the last bullet is a promise, not a demonstration. Our affect! is push!(peak_t, integrator.t), which records and nothing more, so on this deck argmax and the callback would give the same answer. The acting version is Part C of the worksheet, where the same callback drops β when I crosses capacity. Say that rather than implying this code already does it. The corner line at the bottom is the honest caveat, and it runs the other way from the rest of the slide: root-finding is the method that fails there. Exercise 1 in the chapter builds that case. ::: ## `CallbackSet`: more than one event {.smaller} `solve` takes a single `callback =`. The lockdown alone is already two events: ```julia cb = CallbackSet(PresetTimeCallback([t1], start_lockdown!), PresetTimeCallback([t2], end_lockdown!)) ``` - Combines any number of callbacks, discrete and continuous, into one object. - Continuous conditions are root-found first and the earliest crossing applied; discrete callbacks then fire in the order you listed them. - The peak detector could go in the same set. We run it separately here so the peak is measured on the run *without* the intervention. ::: {.notes} This is the composition point of the session in miniature. Each callback was written knowing nothing about the others, and combining them needs no change to either one. Say why the peak detector is kept out of cb: the two are answering different questions. cb asks what the lockdown does; peak_cb asks where the untouched epidemic turns. Putting them in one set would be legitimate, it would just measure the peak of the intervened run instead. ::: ## Julia API: a lockdown & peak detection {.smaller} ::: {#s-ch03-callbacks .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using DiffEqCallbacks t1, t2 = 10.0, 30.0; β_lock = 0.025 set_β!(integ, β) = (integ.p = merge(integ.p, (β = β,))) # NamedTuple stays a NamedTuple cb = CallbackSet(PresetTimeCallback([t1], i -> set_β!(i, β_lock)), PresetTimeCallback([t2], i -> set_β!(i, 0.05))) sol_lock = solve(prob, Tsit5(); callback = cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8) peak_t = Float64[] dIdt(u, p) = (p.β * p.c * u[2] / p.N) * u[1] - p.γ * u[2] # eq-s-ch03-peak peak_cb = ContinuousCallback((u, t, i) -> dIdt(u, i.p), # condition sees u i -> push!(peak_t, i.t)) # affect! sees integrator solve(prob, Tsit5(); callback = peak_cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8) println("peak day (callback): ", round(peak_t[1]; digits = 2)) println("peak I, stored points: ", round(maximum(sol[2, :]); digits = 2)) println("peak I, interpolant: ", round(maximum(sol(t)[2] for t in 0:0.01:80); digits = 2)) println("peak I, lockdown: ", round(maximum(sol_lock[2, :]); digits = 2), " on day ", sol_lock.t[argmax(sol_lock[2, :])], " which in this case does agree with interpolation: ", round(maximum(sol_lock(t)[2] for t in 0:0.01:80); digits = 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` peak day (callback): 17.52 peak I, stored points: 158.34 peak I, interpolant: 158.45 peak I, lockdown: 86.04 on day 10.0 which in this case does agree with interpolation: 86.04 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Read the three numbers as one story: the lockdown roughly halves the peak, 158 down to 86, and after release the rebound only reaches 37. Two details are worth pointing at, both visible on this slide. The peak time comes from root-finding while the peak height comes from stored points, so the height is the less accurate of the two numbers on screen. And day 10 is a corner, not a turning point: this lockdown is strong enough to turn the epidemic the instant it starts, so dI/dt jumps from positive to negative without passing through zero. Run peak_cb on sol_lock and it reports nothing at all. That is the last bullet of the ContinuousCallback slide, and Exercise 1 in the chapter is built on it. ::: ## `remake`: same problem, new numbers {.smaller} A scenario differs from the baseline in one field. Rebuilding the whole problem retypes the three fields that did not change: ```julia scenario = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, merge(p, (β = 0.035,))) # retypes everything scenario = remake(prob; p = merge(p, (β = 0.035,))) # copies, replaces p ``` - `remake` copies a problem and replaces only the fields you name: `p`, `u0`, `tspan`, and the rest. - `prob` itself is untouched, so a sweep over scenarios cannot damage the baseline it is being compared against. - Fitting, sensitivity and inference packages all build their trial problems this way: same kernel, new parameters, thousands of times. ::: {.notes} The argument for remake is not that it saves typing on one line. It is that the scenario stays defined as a difference from the baseline, so when the baseline changes, the scenario follows. Rebuilding by hand duplicates u0 and tspan, and those copies go stale silently. Point out that the parameters here are still built with merge, the same function as in the lockdown affect!. One replaces a field in a NamedTuple, the other replaces a field in a problem. Mention where this returns: in the estimation and inference sessions the optimiser calls remake on every iteration, and in the sensitivity session the ensemble does it per sample. Nobody rebuilds an ODEProblem in a loop. ::: ## One problem, many compatible tools {.smaller} ::: {#cell-s-ch03-composability .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # saveat fixes the output grid, so the algorithms are compared on the same points. peak_I(args...; kw...) = round(maximum(solve(args...; saveat = 0.25, kw...)[2, :]); digits = 1) scenario = remake(prob; p = merge(p, (β = 0.035,))) # same problem, new parameters (tsit = peak_I(prob, Tsit5()), # one algorithm vern = peak_I(prob, Vern7()), # another, same problem lower_β = peak_I(scenario, Tsit5()), # a scenario lockdown = peak_I(prob, Tsit5(); callback = cb)) ``` ::: {#s-ch03-composability .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (tsit = 158.5, vern = 158.5, lower_β = 52.6, lockdown = 86.0) ``` ::: ::: - `ODEProblem` holds the *problem*; the algorithm is chosen separately. - Sensitivity, estimation and inference packages take the same `prob`. ::: {.notes} This is the concrete version of the composability claim asserted in the Julia essentials session. Nothing here is a new model: `prob` and `cb` were built earlier in this deck, and every line reuses them. The mechanism, said plainly: `ODEProblem` stores the scientific problem separately from the algorithm used to solve it. Multiple dispatch examines the types of both the problem and the algorithm and calls a compatible implementation. Other packages build on the same problem and solution types, so there is usually less package-specific conversion code between stages of a workflow. `remake` is the same idea for the data: a new problem that shares everything except what you changed. Give the qualification, because someone will otherwise over-generalise it. Composability does not mean every Julia package automatically works with every other package. It means packages can implement shared interfaces and extend one another without modifying the original package. Where an interface is not shared, you write the glue like anywhere else. Tsit5 and Vern7 agree here because the problem is not stiff; the point is that swapping the algorithm changed one word and no model code. Do not claim a performance win from the swap, there is none to show at this size. ::: ## Generated result ::: {#cell-fig-s-ch03-lockdown .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie tt = 0.0:0.25:80.0 fig = Figure(size = (760, 400)) ax = Axis(fig[1,1]; xlabel = "day", ylabel = "I(t)", title = "SIR with a lockdown") vspan!(ax, t1, t2; color = (:grey, 0.15)) lines!(ax, tt, [sol(t)[2] for t in tt]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "no intervention") lines!(ax, tt, [sol_lock(t)[2] for t in tt]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, linestyle = :dash, label = "lockdown") vlines!(ax, peak_t; color = :black, linestyle = :dot, label = "detected peak") axislegend(ax; position = :rt); fig ``` ::: {#fig-s-ch03-lockdown .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Infectious curve without intervention (red) and with a lockdown halving β over days 10–30 (dashed blue, shaded). The vertical line marks the detected baseline peak. ::: ::: ## Validation Conservation, interpolation self-consistency, and event-detected peak vs a brute-force scan: ::: {#cell-s-ch03-check .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} cons = all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), 1000.0; atol = 1e-6), sol.u) interp = isapprox(sol(sol.t[10]), sol.u[10]; atol = 1e-8) dense_t = 0.0:0.01:80.0 brute = dense_t[argmax([sol(t)[2] for t in dense_t])] peak_ok = isapprox(peak_t[1], brute; atol = 0.05) (cons, interp, peak_ok) ``` ::: {#s-ch03-check .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (true, true, true) ``` ::: ::: All `true`: the solver conserves population, its interpolant is faithful, and the callback peak matches the maximum. ## Limitations & takeaways {.smaller} **What the workflow separates** - *What the model is* (`ODEProblem`), *how it is solved* (`Tsit5`, tolerances), and *what happens during* the solve (callbacks) are three independent choices. - Swap the algorithm or `remake` a scenario, with no change to the model. - Callbacks turn an integrator into an event-driven simulator. **What to be careful about** - Report numbers from `sol(t)`, not from stored points: 158.34 against 158.45 here. - The model inherits every SIR assumption: homogeneous mixing, continuous state, memoryless recovery. - The lockdown is a perfect switch. In reality, the adherence to a policy is gradual, noisy, and responds to the epidemic. **Takeaway:** learn `ODEProblem` + solver + callbacks once, reuse it everywhere. ::: {.notes} The corner bullet is the one to slow down on, because it is the only limitation here that this session demonstrated rather than asserted. Point back at slide 10: the lockdown peak printed as 86.04 on day 10.0, exactly the switching time. Run peak_cb on that solution and it returns an empty vector. Exercise 1 in the chapter builds the case, and the fix is to check t₁, t₂ and both ends of the span alongside whatever root-finding reports. Each item in the SIR list names a later session, so use it as the map: jump processes for stochastic extinction and integer counts, SDEs for noise, agent based models for mixing. Memoryless recovery is the exponential infectious period, which the delay appendix relaxes. Realistic interventions involve uncertainty and feedback, deferred to the interventions and control chapter. Invite learners to sweep β_lock in the notebook. ::: ## Next: ::: {style="margin-top: 3.5em;"} - Go to the worksheet folder and open the `chapters/03-ordinary-differential-equations.qmd` worksheet. - Follow the instructions and complete the exercises. - Let us know if you have any questions! :::
